Unlike previous studies that utilized meaning-based pre-training for reading comprehension, we adapt and refine this concept to understand conversational contexts, leveraging context-aware conversation symptoms to define high-quality training targets. We develop the MeaningAMBERT model by incorporating meaning-based symptoms into pre-training, which outperforms other models on managing parasitic conversational contexts, according to assessment by human judges. Furthermore, our study compares MeaningAMBERT with other pre-trained models, including BERT and SMART, on conversational response generation, achieving notable improvements in ROUGE metrics.

Machine learning algorithms have become ubiquitous and are now used in a variety of situations. However, their ability to make predictions doesn't necessarily mean they are understandable. Explainable AI, on the other hand, involves the area of machine learning that focuses on making its processes more transparent. From this perspective, the key to developing effective learning systems lies not only in creating algorithms that can produce accurate outcomes, but also ones that are easy to learn and adapt. This study puts forward a comprehensive framework for measuring the interpretability of algorithms in relation to how well they can be learned by humans. The research also proposes a specific metric for assessing interpretability, known as the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS), which gauges complexity using factors such as clarity of goals, simplicity of decision-making processes, and consistency in actions. CCS is a quantifiable property that can be used to evaluate and compare the interpretability of diverse machine learning models, for example, those based on different approaches or designed for different types of knowledge. This study's findings are rooted in a large-scale learning experiment in which 336 subjects learned to control their agents either with random algorithms, either due to the experiment's design, either because the algorithm's goals and rules for action were clearly communicated to them), or based on an optimally designed teaching approach (with gradual increases in difficulty and clear explanation of goals and rules as needed). The study's key discovery is that algorithmic transparency and explainability, though crucial for learning, are not the only essential factors

This paper presents an adapted version of the Isolation Forest algorithm, tailored for use with imbalanced and minute machine learning models. The algorithm was incorporated into a system utilizing TiWS, a protocol for efficiently transmitting weak signals containing annotation-free data between devices. The adapted Isolation Forest algorithm was applied to data obtained from a TiWS experiment, with results indicating its effectiveness in pinpointing anomalies within the data. Furthermore, the study showcases the capabilities of a custom-made camera application developed for Android and iOS platforms, enabling real-time identification of anomalies directly from visual inputs.

This research proposes a novel approach to parameterize the extremal index under a Bayesian framework. By assuming that a sequence of time-stamped extreme events forms a Poisson process, we derive the extremal index in terms of average inter-arrival times. Utilizing a t-transformation for these times enables us to apply Bayesian inference, incorporating prior knowledge on $\tau_0$ and enabling comparisons across different studies. A test-case simulation reveals that our proposed method successfully captures the relationship between $\tau_0$ and itself, and between $\tau_0$ and sample size. Additionally, we apply this technique to estimate the extremal index for both simulated data and real-world instances of phosphate stormwater runoff data in urban environments.

In pair production processes, the conditions under which the cross section will remain constant need to be investigated. For this purpose, partial wave expansion is employed for the electroweak gauge bosinosafter relativistic propagation in a plane wave, yielding matrix elements in terms of target momentum. These terms are then used to calculate cross sections through the L\"uders diagram, demonstrating that the cross section comprises the tendency of the virtual boson to break up into a pair, as well as the tendency of the pair to coalesce into a virtual boson. The former is simply the geometric cross section of the pair, and it is shown that the cross section remains constant for nonrelativistic kinematics, moderate values of target momentum, and certain regions of large momentum transfer. For nonrelativistic kinematics, the constant areas are found to be circular; for moderate momentum, these areas are also circular but possess center values different from zero; and for certain regions of large momentum transfer, these areas are also circular with center values different from zero. For relativistic kinematics, the constant areas are not only circular but also vary in radius based on momentum. For pairs consisting of vector bosons, the constant areas not only depend on momentum but also exhibit symmetry properties based on cosmological parity.

The COMET-ATOMIC dataset, an extensive collection of everyday relational facts, was first introduced in 2019. This dataset, comprised of nearly 240K relationship statements, is derived from ATOMIC, a vast dataset containing over 7 million atomic relational facts, was initially depicted as being generated through crowdsourcing. This paper reveals that COMET-ATOMIC is actually a tokenized version of the symbolic knowledge graph within ATOMIC, is indexed for efficient query processing, and is designed both to facilitate rapid information retrieval and to bolster the development of artificial intelligence models capable of learning through reinforcement. As such, COMET-ATOMIC 2020 is positioned as a competition that showcases state-of-the-art machine learning capabilities for entity embedding and knowledge graph indexing techniques, with a primary goal of determining which of these methodologies is better equipped to handle common sense knowledge at scale. Competitors were tasked with developing accurate representations of entities within the COMET-ATOMIC dataset, with results being reflected through both a primary evaluation metric that assesses overall knowledge coverage and a secondary evaluation metric that focuses on individual knowledge assertions. Ultimately, the competition yielded four neural network entity embedding methods, one symbolic knowledge graph indexing approach, and two hybrid methodologies that combine the efficacy of both. It is anticipated that the data, evaluation methods, and findings derived from this competition will contribute significantly to the collective understanding of the field, with results demonstrating that COMET-ATOMIC 2020 was both a defining moment for the development of everyday

The initial release of processed Hi-GAL data, based on $eml$ expressions and cloud recognition algorithms, is detailed. These outputs were generated using the EMCEE-3D/Unsharp2 tool and are foundational for future research on compact clouds, filaments, and outflows. They are specifically designed for analysis using the APERO tool but can also be utilized directly, offering advantages such as reduced data size (factor of 10) and compressed image formats (factor of 100). APERO can further leverage these outputs to create interactive images. Moreover, the pipeline includes specific provisions for individual research objects, including outflows, proto-stellar clouds, and specific sources like CB108 in Taurus, which serves as a test case. Ultimately, the pipeline allows for the customization of derived scientific products through the selection of specific criteria, leading to the creation of new research opportunities.

The Milky Way's inner regions, being located near the galaxy's center, are exposed to an older (13 billion-year-old), low-metal content star population. A study focused on the globular cluster NGC 2808, rich in this type of star, aimed at analyzing key characteristics, revealing an unusual spread in metal content. An examination of 1,516 NGC 2808 stars with detailed spectral analysis, along with temperature and luminosity measurements, allowed us to calculate essential properties such as size, mass, and surface gravity. Additionally, we analyzed the movement patterns of these stars, discovering two distinct groups. By applying specific filters to eliminate blue, young stars, we were able to compare our results with existing data, further validating our findings. A separate study focused on 246 bright stars within the same cluster provided even more precise information on their metal content, metal composition, and age. This extensive analysis confirms that NGC 2808 consists of two distinct metal content groups, consisting of 75% (metal-poor) and 25% (metal-rich) populations, further highlighting the presence of these groups through horizontal Branch morphology. We were also able to rule out possible explanations for these different populations, such as stellar evolution or variations in star formation patterns. Further investigation into the possible explanations behind these different populations remains an area for future research.

When a priced service becomes free of charge, as with free Wi-Fi, users may initially rush to take advantage of the discounted offer.  During this promotional period, the initial exit time $T$ follows an exponential distribution, with $\mathcal{T} \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$, and in the process, the rate $\lambda$ characterizes how quickly customers leave after obtaining the service for free. As more users gain access to the service, the initial exit rate $\lambda$ decreases, indicating that once the service is in high demand, users no longer rush to sign up as they can simply wait for a spot to become available.  With $\lambda$ directly related to the entropy of the initial distribution, the problem explores how the initial exit duration is connected to the entropic power.  Assuming that the initial waiting time for the service is a Poisson process, the problem explores the relationship between the high demand waiting times and the initial exit duration.  Using the properties of the Gamma distribution, the problem explores how the initial waiting time is related to the service price.

Quantum Bayes' Theorem has been consistently proving useful in understanding how to apply classical Bayes methods within the context of quantum settings. One common misconception surrounding this area of research posits that quantum features like superposition and entanglement negatively impact the traditional concept of probability. In reality, this work aims to demonstrate the opposite: that strong, global coherence in the initial state significantly contributes to accurate inference results. To support this claim, we set out to quantify coherence, one of the primary aspects associated with entanglement, using the index of coherence $C\rho(\gamma)$. Our analysis focuses on the quantum version of Bayes' Theorem in relation to entangled photon pairs, where we use the index of coherence to better understand how entropy influences the prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we also look at how entropy affects the prediction accuracy in two distinct scenarios. Our analysis reveals that entanglement plays a pivotal role in ensuring reliable predictions.

In high-energy situations, quantum chromodynamics (QCD) behaves differently when describing the properties of quarks and gluons in terms of their momentum densities. To address this, a new mathematical formula for energy density, pressure, and mass density has been developed for small numbers of particles, taking into account the complex interactions of gluons. This approach has been expressed in terms of a basic building block, allowing for a reliable calculation of QCD properties across a wide range of densities. This range includes densities that are lower than what is typically seen in the early stages of hadron formation, but also higher than what is typically associated with multi-hadron systems. Applying this framework, we calculated the mass density, energy density, and pressure of a quark-gluon gas in small groups, discovering a distinct phase where the relationship between pressure and energy is particularly close. This phenomenon turns out to be a general feature of systems with self-interacting gluons, and it implies that certain mathematical formulas commonly applied in high-energy situations are actually valid in low-energy contexts as well. The strength of gluon interactions also determines when this mathematical effect becomes noticeable, and it's as strong as the typical strength of gluon interactions suggests. Our findings have significant implications for the study of heavy, compositionally simple objects where general formulas may break down due to complex interactions.

The Steenrod algebra's $A($$E4)$ cohomology generation is well-established for $E4$-based unstable coalgebras with simple components in cohomology. This new work takes this concept further, giving an $E4$-based classification for unstable virtual mod $2$ extensions of the Steenrod algebra, focusing on cohomology with decomposable components. As a result, we can restate the Cohen-MacLachlan-Luecking Theorem using $E4$-based terminology, while also providing an example that demonstrates the existence of a non-trivial extended algebra with trivial action but still basic for $A($$E4)$. This example contrasts with existing results for the simple components in cohomology of the Steenrod algebra.

Researchers working in Lyman ultraviolet astronomy are facing significant challenges due to high scatter and signal interference from Lyman-alpha radiation. Current correction methods, such as using Lyman-alpha filters, are limited in their effectiveness below wavelength 365 nm. A new approach involves incorporating a LISA-like UV/350 nm camera into Lyman ultraviolet spectrographics and photometers to provide improved precision. This improved precision would enable broader applications in various astronomical contexts including star, planet, and galaxy observations. By combining the LISA filter with a precision Lyot stellar array, the LISA-like camera can accurately remove Lyman-alpha interference across the entire Lyman band, allowing for the exploration of critical hydrogen absorption in high-redshift galaxies and quasi-stellar objects. By combining this with existing technologies such as UV spectrographics, the LISA-like camera can facilitate groundbreaking observations in the far ultraviolet spectrum of quasi-stellar objects and galaxy nuclei, and provide new insights into the star formation history of the universe, including supernova explosion mechanisms and late-time star evolution.

This paper addresses the problem of identifying, clustering, and managing network graphs, specifically those that exhibit symmetry, to enhance overall network performance. Currently available methods for graph partitioning are focused on optimizing specific network properties but lack a broad understanding of symmetry. In contrast, our proposed approach leverages recent developments in distributed computing to create a general framework for capturing and applying symmetry in enhanced graph algorithms.

This paper presents a method for cataloging images that incorporates new data and adapts to changes in image sources and labels. Conventional image catalogs built using static datasets like ImageNet overlook shifts in image distributions and class label changes, hindering their performance in real-world applications. Our approach addresses this shortcoming by developing a dynamic image catalog framework that incorporates data drift detection and adapts to distribution shifts and evolving label distributions. For data drift detection, we utilize an uncertainty-based method, leveraging neural network predictions to pinpoint regions of interest and identify distribution shifts. For distribution adaptation, we employ a domain adaptation technique that removes the influence of image statistics specific to each domain, effectively transferring image representations to a common space. For label adaptation, we develop a Bayesian technique that aggregates label distributions from multiple sources, aiming to accurately compile image-class label matrices. For instance, when compiling a Sunflower-image class-label matrix, our method aggregates distributions from multiple sources, accurately increasing performance to 80.4%. Similarly, applying our method to a pairwise dataset performs on par with or better than existing methods in image domain adaptation, removing task-irrelevant information.

This study verifies the existence of a blind key generation process through local randomness extraction in memoryless, discrete, and inseparable sources over the Gaussian channel, following a 2017 theorem by Li et al. Initially, a lower bound on local randomness extraction rate is established for such sources, based on a total conditional variance measure. It is then demonstrated how this variance measure may also serve as an effective test for determining whether two paired sources of discrete memoryless pairs are statistically independent, uncoupled, and uniquely correlated. Utilizing this local randomness extraction concept, a lower bound on the rate of secret key generation for sources adhering to these criteria is then mathematically defined. It is also shown that in order to achieve this lower bound, it is sufficient to have the locally derived sources of random code sequences possess a total conditional variance measure less than a specific threshold. Furthermore, it is noted that such a threshold exists when the sources of random code sequences possess a total conditional variance measure less than or equal to $2/3$.

A particle moves without dispersion when its wave function remains unchanged under Poincaré's group, specifically the translation operator. In this work, we explore Poincaré invariance in one-dimensional systems under discrete (quantized) washboard potentials. We find that, uniquely, the bound states of the canonical sawtooth potential exhibit Poincaré invariance. We extend our analysis to higher-dimensional generalizations of these potentials and identify specific conditions, related to symmetry, for achieving dispersion-free motion. We also demonstrate that, beyond sawtooth, there are other "dispersion-free" potentials, resulting from quantized, cyclic translations of position. These include stepped, shifted sawtooth, shifted sinusoidal, and "bent" potentials. We further establish a link between these potential types through canonical relations, analogous to Darboux' duality, quantized by unitary equivalence. Moreover, we develop metric structures on these "dispersion-free" spaces, enabling geodesic motion that itself remains dispersion-free. We conclude by presenting potential applications of these ideas, including novel quantum computing architectures.

This research introduces enhanced, flexible versions of the SahaTkati algorithm for
processing impulse response data, including a version capable of utilizing
interpolated data points and another for handling irregularly spaced data points.
We also present a novel version of the algorithm designed for making predictions
on a grid of points without requiring a function to be evaluated at those
specific points. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the ADAPT function, which
adapts to a polynomial of a specified degree, can efficiently interpolate
empirically constructed impulse responses, even when processing Irregularly spaced
data. Moreover, ADAPT produces accurate predictions on a grid of points using
less than the original data points, which can also be irregularly spaced. This is
then applied to empirical impulse responses from GDS-IV, which reveals that the VEC
model specification produces results similar to those of the TF-SVAR model in
terms of recovering the true impulse responses in a data-generated study. However,
the GDS-IV method has the significant advantage of only utilizing half of the data
points, including the single observation at t=0, to produce results. This is in
addition to ADAPT making this possible without sacrificing its accuracy.

In this study, we have made an assessment of quantum void phenomena and found that the magnitude of the induced electric dipole moment creates a distinction between particles with angular quantum numbers greater than or equal to 2 and those with lower angular numbers. Consequently, our analysis focuses on a specific case involving a 2D quantum particle subjected to a constant magnetic field and positioned in a superposition of states with angular number 2. When this particle interacts with a photon in the magnetic field, our results show that the time it takes for the particle to develop a non-zero induced electric dipole moment increases significantly as the particle's reduced Planck constant becomes very small. Notably, our results also reveal that the magnitude of the induced electric dipole moment, when the particle has a non-zero momentum, decreases significantly in comparison to the classic result under the same conditions.

Research in AI's subfield of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has highlighted the benefits of hierarchical knowledge representation in addressing the challenges of knowledge organization and retrieval. In this context, hierarchical knowledge representation involves connecting related concepts to their more specific subcategories, which is a fundamental aspect of knowledge graph engineering. A key challenge in maintaining such graphs lies in annotating the edges with meaningful labels that reflect their semantic relationships. Recent studies have shown that hyperbolic graph learning can effectively address this issue by leveraging the inherent hierarchical properties of data. Specifically, a novel approach called FGNET-RH (Folger Graph with Neural Tree - Recursive Hierarchical) has been proposed for labeled edge prediction in hyperbolic space. By incorporating a recursive neural tree model, FGNET-RH seamlessly integrates parent node features with child node characteristics to enhance its predictions. To improve its performance, FGNET-RH also utilizes a custom-designed loss function that promotes the convergence of distant tree nodes towards a common optimal direction. Comprehensive experiments on the Folger Graph benchmark demonstrate the superior performance of FGNET-RH by achieving a significant 12.7% improvement in edge prediction accuracy compared to a leading alternative method, while showcasing a substantial 52.5% increase in performance over a recently proposed yet inefficient baseline approach.

This paper explores special properties of the second Hankel determinant for a specific class of entire functions without positive zeros, utilizing the iterative method to derive formulas and establish inequalities, and reveals that $h_2(n)$ can take on both the smallest and largest possible values. Furthermore, we investigate an open problem and prove that $h_2(n)$ cannot achieve certain values, while also developing a comprehensive model to analyze its behavior.

In a cloud-based environment with a data hub, multiple virtual machines (VMs) likely exist to accommodate different services and data storage, where each service and data instance demands exclusive access to at least one host node. These services and data instances vary in their scheduling strategies depending on their complexity, including some that require allocation across entire nodes while others necessitate distribution across multiple nodes with distributed data. To manage VM allocations in this data hub framework, we introduce Prepartition - a load distribution method designed to facilitate the allocation of VMs with varied scheduling demands. Prepartition is characterized by two key features: first, it mirrors the scheduling requirements of complex services and data instances by dividing load into components and distributing them across subnodes, thus facilitating efficient allocations that minimize overall load through dynamic adjustment of subnodes; second, it allows load to be mapped to specific host nodes based on service and data class demands to ensure effective load distribution, balanced host utilization, and reduced load variability. Our evaluation using real data hub services and data instances demonstrates that Prepartition outperforms existing load distribution methods, delivering more consistent results.

We're working with a large set of games, specifically 2x2 games, to develop forecasting models that can accurately predict the most likely outcomes. These models, built on the 'Fixed Point Networks' architecture, produce equitable predictions by leveraging fixed point methods. We'll use preliminary results to illustrate the challenges in equilibriums prediction and how our approach outperforms existing solutions. Furthermore, additional findings will show the effectiveness of a novel loss function in generating equitable forecasts. Lastly, we'll examine potential weaknesses of our model when confronted with data lacking equitative properties.

We focus on identifying the effects of interventions in a discrete random variable system. Using a high-dimensional dataset, we aim to measure its partial correlation matrix based on observed data only, unlike in high-dimensional statistical analysis where we work under specific distribution assumptions. Working within a high-dimensional framework characterized by a large number of variables relative to sample size, we generate estimators for the partial correlation matrix based solely on causal discovery techniques. In this framework, we extend the Helveck inequality to derive concentration bounds for any symmetric positive semi-definite estimator. Furthermore, we generate sample size requirements for achieving tight bounds in high-dimensional applications. We apply these results to analyze a Google dataset involving over 170 million Android app installations, examining how user interactions influence installation rates for demo apps. In this context, we identify interesting findings such as the presence of apparent causal relations (e.g., the presence of an ad indicator reducing the likelihood of an app being installed) as well as more complex connections (e.g., the likelihood of an app being installed conditional on the frequency of user's actions).

This study addresses the issue of using surveillance without indication in the control of systems that behave linearly. These systems may be subject to secret manipulation of their readings by an adversary. There has been previous research on this topic, with one approach involving setting a threshold above which a warning is triggered. However, this method has limitations as it only detects attacks after they have occurred and fails to account for the impact on system performance. In contrast, our proposed strategy involves setting thresholds that balance detection and response to attacks while minimizing the impact on system performance during unattacked periods. This goal is achieved by incorporating key performance indicators and utilizing robust statistics from the most susceptible components to establish thresholds. Specifically, our approach sets output, state, and input thresholds beyond the point of attack feasibility. To determine these thresholds, we formulate an optimization problem that addresses performance during attacks and robustness during normal conditions. This method relies on estimates to establish thresholds, and its effectiveness is evaluated using simulations on a system model.

Summarization is a vital task in natural language processing that enables text condensation, making information consumption more accessible and efficient for readers. Traditional summarization methods based on textual features have been widely explored, but recent studies have shown that incorporating graph structural information can significantly enhance performance. Despite the effectiveness of existing graph-based approaches, they often require training data to design the underlying graph structure. This limitation is particularly noticeable when dealing with datasets that are small, irregular, or uncommon, hindering their applicability. To address this issue, our study introduces a novel graph structure that is more adaptable to diverse datasets, thereby allowing for its use without training on specific information. The graph structure in question is based on the idea of interconnected nodes representing similar text segments through common content, and it is defined by a similarity measure over the text content automatically extracted from the input document. This discovery enables us to develop an unsupervised graph aided summarization system that is model-independent and exemplified by its successful application in summarizing information contained within Indian languages where the graph structure is particularly useful due to its limited availability, and also other low resource languages.

We introduce the concept of S-rings of the Noetherian type, distinct from standard rings, and carry out classification by establishing the standard list of creation operators for any such S-ring. Furthermore, an explicit list of standard lists for Noetherian S-rings is provided. These results are then applied to a new classification of finite S-rings according to their standard lists' length. Additionally, the set consisting of finite S-rings of Noetherian type paired with finite standard lists is identified.

Recent research has revealed a high rate of unseen companions among rapidly accelerating stars. This study aimed to discover and analyze the characteristics of these unseen companions in a sample of five such stars. We utilized a sophisticated statistical model combined with the RAND search method to drill down on the possibilities. Our findings include the detection of a companion near the star G239-42, with an estimated mass between 0.083 to 0.197 times the mass of the sun located approximately 2.67 to 3.15 times the star's radius. Furthermore, the data suggest the companion is likely in a circular orbit. In contrast, the system of the star G228-19 is clear of any significant information on an accompanying companion. We were unsuccessful in identifying the companion surrounding the star G155-35, the system G166-19, or the system G189-51.

Recent research has introduced constrained variational Bayesian autoencoders.  This paper examines the minimization of a divergent upper bound in a specific type of such models.  We show that the optimized restricted variation in a Gaussian distribution is exactly 1 plus the logarithm of the ratio between 2 sigma squared delta and 2 sigma delta, where delta represents the difference between the expected value and the true value.  We discovered that the optimized restricted variation in a Bernoulli distribution is exactly 1 plus the logarithm of the ratio between 1 minus 2 p delta and 2 delta, where p represents the expected value.  We compare the generalization performance of such models with standard variational autoencoders.

This study presents a novel method to identify location and track moving objects within a confined area, such as intelligent home spaces equipped with IoT systems and a private blockchain network. A cutting-edge device, like the Raspberry Pi, is utilized to develop a GPS-based positioning system with the capacity for accurate, real-time 2D positioning. A private blockchain network incorporating smart contracts seamlessly integrates with this system, enabling efficient tracking of objects within the space. A thorough examination is conducted to assess the performance of this positioning system under different GPS satellite configurations and environmental influences. The analysis validates the effectiveness and precision of this method in tracking objects.

A widely used still-image compression technique, difference modulation (DM), has the advantage of offering dynamic range adaptation without pre-knowing the receiver's display characteristics. Its method of quantizing L-value luminance information involves dividing it into intervals and representing them with a fixed number of bits. This paper proposes an improved approach where each L-value is individually encoded using an adaptive number of bits based on its magnitude. To achieve this, we trained neural networks to predict probability distributions for each possible number of bits. The results show that our technique surpasses the traditional L-value quantization method in rate-distortion performance. Furthermore, we discovered that by applying a form of data augmentation from the reinforcement learning framework, we can significantly decrease the size of the models required to achieve the same performance.

This study focuses on parameterized assessments of finding optimal solutions to Upward Planarity. Building on Bulles and Schaefer's 2017 findings that identified approach complexity parameters to determine when an Upward Planarity with bounded aspect ratio could be solved efficiently, this research enhances those results by identifying specific, more refined approach complexity parameters that apply to the problem. The new parameters will allow for even more refined evaluations of the problem's efficiency in the future.

Previous research has highlighted the dangers of relying on synthetic data, including introducing errors that can be detrimental to model performance. Nonetheless, leveraging crowdsourced data through machine learning holds significant potential, especially in supplementing scarce datasets to mitigate imbalances. This balancing act can be accomplished by employing data sampling methods to create representative datasets. Moreover, using Bayesian techniques to incorporate uncertainty into model design helps to accurately interpret output predictions and prevents models from making false assurances. This confidence information can also be utilized to post-hoc evaluate dataset quality, including crowdsourced data. This research proposes an ensemble modeling framework that utilizes the human softmax model to determine which sources - in this case, crowdworkers - provide reliable data and should therefore be included in the training process. The framework co-opts multiple pre-existing models, calculates their respective output distributions, and assembles a new human-centric dataset based on the combinations of these distributions, cross-validated to ensure consistency across human agents. The framework further fine-tunes model performance using an entropy-based metric to assess and mitigate dataset biases resulting from crowdworkers' inconsistent behavior. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of our method through experiments on datasets collected through both crowdworkers and real-world users, showcasing its potential to accurately assess and utilize the reliability of both sources.

This study examines the norm diminution in a broad context involving transfer operators associated with nonuniform hyperbolic semiflows, covering both the uniform and nonuniform settings, across various domains including real and complex spaces, with a focus on conditions ensuring the $L^p$ norm diminution holds for $p$ in the interval $[1,\infty)$. A key aspect of this research is its application to nonuniform hyperbolic semiflows that exhibit significant exponential dilations in compact subdomains. Additionally, it is demonstrated that $L^p$ bounded transfer operators exist for semiflows with exponential dilations in compact subdomains for any $p$ in the interval $(1,\infty)$. As a result, the research provides the creation of new classes of transfer operators including those associated with real and complex semiflows as well as those with domains defined as the union of multiple domains.

A special matrix known as a covering array, with certain properties, is used to assign tasks in a way that uses the least number of rows. This idea was first introduced by J. J. Denes and A. Beral in 1959. Since then, there have been various studies on optimal and near-optimal covering arrays. One type of covering array, known as strength-$2$, is used in situations where there are interdependencies between different tasks. A recent paper by J. J. Wang, et al., discussed a type of tiny covering arrays, with good performance in size and number of columns. This paper uses the same concept of tiny strength-$2$ covering arrays to explore new methods of covering arrays, particularly in situations with many tasks and few columns. By redefining the concept of tiny, and using different parameters, new lower bounds on covering arrays are established. Several examples are given to demonstrate the improvement in size of tiny covering arrays for certain combinations of parameters.
In a competition where performance and luck are perfectly linked, simultaneous ranking of players using observation of only two players at a time is impossible.

This study involves a controlled replication and expansion of a 2019 algorithm designed to automatically reproduce software faults identified in Intelligent Textual Normalization (ITN) data. As a part of the Replication Genome project, this algorithm was tested and refined using a full dataset, contrasting a previous trial that employed a subset of the data. Initially deployed on a subset of 106 failures, this algorithm demonstrated minimal precision in reproducing fault instances. With the goal of increasing effectiveness, this algorithm's parameters were readapted for new trials on larger, combined datasets. Ultimately, this involved testing the algorithm on a combined dataset of 259 failures. Both successful and faulty outputs were analyzed to determine the accuracy of fault reproduction, with the results showing a substantial enhancement in mean absolute error compared to the initial deployment.

The unusual "fisheyes" in vortices within high-temperature cuprate superconductors have long captivated the attention of researchers due to their intricate structures. Despite extensive research, the underlying causes for these intricate patterns remain unclear in low and intermediate magnetic fields. Our study presents new findings on the interlocked square patterns within fisheyes in Nd-doped La cuprate that exhibit unique properties in low and intermediate magnetic fields. Our detailed investigations show that these patterns arise from square arrangements of quanta of magnetic flux when the magnetic field direction is close to parallel to the superconductor's surface. By carefully increasing the strength of the magnetic field, we observed that the patterns transition from square to circular shapes with characteristic "eyes." Our observations suggest that the intricate patterns within fisheyes change type depending on the direction of the magnetic field with respect to the surface of the superconductor, leading to complex shapes characterized by four symmetric arms and a central circular area. Our study demonstrates that the fisheyes can display different types of symmetry and pattern depending on the angle of the magnetic field with respect to the surface of the superconductor, and that these patterns within fisheyes can be replicated through simulation of superconductivity in a planar material system.

Research at RHIC and LHC reveals that protons can form complex, soup-like states at extremely high temperatures and density.  Observations of early particle formation indicate the formation of such complex states in high-energy collisions.  However, due to limitations in detecting these particles, the development of such states is still not fully understood and can only be analyzed through indirect methods.  One of the proposed methods to study the properties of these complex states involves using formed particles to probe its structure.  A recent study found that high-energy $e+e+$ photons produced at mid-rapidity in certain types of collisions exhibit an anisotropic pattern of distribution, which can serve as an indicator of how fluid-like these complex states are.  Data collected during experiments at the PHENIX, PHOSPHORUS, and ALICE detected a significant anisotropic pattern at low energy densities that correlates with this states' viscosity.  A comparison of these findings with theoretical models showed that as energy density decreases, the complex states behave more like ideal liquids.  A future experiment at the FB at the RHIC will further study this relationship during South-North collisions to confirm these initial findings.

For Heisenberg antiferromagnets on triangular and kagome lattices, we've identified common magnetic patterns using exact ground states, and found a method to calculate their partition functions, which confirms the established findings about the energy density for triangular lattices and reveals a method to compute the energy density for kagome lattices, determined by a few key configurations. Analyzing the boundary conditions' impact on kagome lattices shows that as the perimeter grows, the energy density converges towards a certain value, which we determined and compared to findings from numerical simulations.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in discovering interventions' causal effects from observational data, but determining which interventions are most effective remains a challenging task due to the limitations of current methods. Often, researchers rely on costly trial-and-error approaches, resulting in unreliable results and limited insights for future causal inquiries. To address this issue, we focus on identifying intervention-driven causal effects using pairwise comparisons. A novel algorithm, called TIE, is developed to handle the complexity of dependent data while maintaining a statistically-controlled false discovery rate without compromising its power. The efficacy of TIE is demonstrated in our in-depth experimental analysis which includes a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, leading to a significantly higher discovery rate of valid causal effects, thus outperforming the state-of-the-art methods. The source code for TIE is available for public access on our maintained GitHub platform.

We present a cosmological model that incorporates an inflating medium to explain both the rapid expansion of the Universe in the early stages and the current accelerated expansion. A previously established model from [arXiv:1209.6708] provided the foundation for this concept. In this framework, we examine the one-fluid model consisting of dark fluid, dark matter, and the inflating medium, using the deceleration parameter $q$ to investigate the early stages of expansion. Subsequently, we investigate the one-fluid model with respect to deceleration parameters when considering three components: dark fluid, the inflating medium, and radiation. Additionally, we include an electro-magnetic component in the fluid equation to simulate observed patterns from [arXiv:1302.1704, arXiv:1303.5032, arXiv:1401.6674, arXiv:1504.05530, arXiv:1602.02281, arXiv:1608.02906, arXiv:1703.06160, arXiv:1705.17049, arXIV:1803.97.13], assuming homogeneous and isotropic spacetime described by the Friedmann-Lemaitre model.

Using a novel approach to the type-X two Higgs doublet model, we have revisited the type-X 2HDM in light of the latest muon anomalous magnetic moment results. We have analyzed how different ranges of $\lambda_5$ and $\lambda_6$ affect the type-X 2HDM in light of these new findings. Furthermore, our model's predictions for lepton flavor universality violation in $W$ boson decays have been scrutinized by examining the $W$-lepton coupling modification, which manifests as a $O(\frac{m_l}{m_W})$ correction, resulting in a significant impact when combined with the given $W$-lepton coupling. We have also plotted the type-X 2HDM's predictions for $\Delta m_W$ in terms of $\tan\beta$ and $\lambda_5$ as well as $\lambda_6$.

To enhance concept-based search, a task called Quick Automatic Related Search (QUICKAR) aims to identify semantically connected concepts through reformulated reference queries. By leveraging crowdsourced data associated with WordNet, we developed a method to predict concept relationships. Based on these connections, we employ a transformation-based approach to reformulate the original query into a related one. Experiments using human-annotated data from the Visual Genome dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in finding relevant concepts, particularly in search queries with fewer than ten words.

The second iteration of an online platform, known as RCSEDv2, has been developed to facilitate the analysis and visualization of data derived from imaging and spectroscopy, which are grounded in a standard spectral energy distribution. This tool is a progression from its predecessor, RCSED, and is comprised of two applications, SPEDE and Atlas, which are both open-source and freely accessible. SPEDE enables users to create custom spectral energy distributions, which can be used to generate various plots and datasets, including light curves, spectra, and images, all of which are aligned with established astronomical catalogs and databases. Atlas is a data visualization tool that allows users to generate images and spectra based on input data, which can be used to create customized Atlases with predefined boundaries and spectral energy distributions. Both applications include a data browser that enables users to browse and select data, which can also serve as a data analyzer to identify trends and correlations, which are then displayed as interactive plots. Both SPEDE and Atlas are designed to be used in conjunction with web browsers, which can also serve as data analysis and visualization tools, as demonstrated by their usage in the analysis of various astronomical observations, including data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, as part of a virtual workshop.

This project tackles the challenge of unsupervised temporal action segmentation from annotated video data with sparse, imprecise labels. A proposed method, Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP), addresses the issue of sparse annotations by focusing on dense, self-supervised activity patterns in video sequences. It aims to derive fine-grained, compact representations for activity streams through self-supervised learning, using a novel, streamlined co-occurrence parsing model for dense activity pattern extraction. To improve sparse annotation issues, SSCAP incorporates a cross-modal cross-teacher learning approach for shared learning between dense and sparse modalities during training. Cross-modal and cross-teacher knowledge is also transferred from the dense to the sparse modality for learning on the target sparse dataset, with precision-enhanced prediction made on the sparse dataset alone. Evaluation on multiple high-level vision benchmarks demonstrates SSCAP's performance with annotated sparse labels only at a high level, showing significant improvement over existing methods, with code and pre-trained models available on the SSCAP GitHub repository, https://github.com/NovoxSSCAP/SSCAP.

Utilizing the commutator method, we derive the leading terms in the Regge trajectory of $P_c(4450)$ and $P_c(4440)$ states and identify their underlying quarkonia components. In the $P_c(4450)$ state, we determine three quarkonia components, whereas the $P_c(4440)$ state is composed of two quarkonia components. We compare our findings with existing experimental data available in the literature.

Educating future professionals in software testing is a complex endeavor that poses difficulties for instructors, particularly those new to the field. The reasons for this are far-reaching and varied, but essentially, there is a discrepancy between theoretical knowledge and practical application in the area of software testing. This gap exists due to a lack of understanding among students, who possess only partial knowledge in this field, as well as insufficient guidance from instructors in addressing the intricacies involved. 

To address this understanding gap, instructors in software testing provide students with distinct forms of feedback. Two common techniques used include conventional detailed feedback and inquiry-based conceptual feedback. While conventional feedback is primarily centered on reviewing specific tasks, conceptual feedback is focused on enhancing students' fundamental understanding of a subject. 

Empirical research conducted into the use of these methods has found that conceptual feedback is more effective in preventing students' ignorance of software testing fundamentals, ultimately allowing them to demonstrate greater expertise in testing practices, even when using the same tools for assessment. Furthermore, conceptual feedback facilitates learning at an exceptional level, with results being remarkably robust and long-lasting. 

By contrast, effective utilization of conventional feedback requires continuous monitoring from instructors, only yields modest outcomes, and tends to erode over time. 

This study is based on a teaching experience with master's level students in a Fundamentals of Software Testing course, utilizing a case study approach that also involved a survey with fellow professors in the field, comparing student outcomes from an individual and group assessment perspective in relation to the feedback approach

Adjusting adjustments to adapt better to new environments is vital for many areas, yet it tends to be very costly to collect measurements from every single scenario. A potential solution is to employ domain-invariant training, however current strategies usually depend on considerable supervision from the new environment, which can be very expensive or simply impractical. In this context, we introduce Semi-Supervised Domain Adjustment, a method that exploits unlabeled data from the new environment and previous knowledge to learn a more effective mapping between the two domains without requiring considerable supervision from the new environment. A key challenge is the scarcity of labeled data, so we implement a technique that blends knowledge transfer with semi-supervised learning to overcome this issue. Experiment results on different domain adjustment tasks confirm that our approach achieves source-free performance comparable to the supervised alternative, outperforms other strategies that are semi-supervised yet require considerable domain-specific data, and even surpasses partially domain-invariant training strategies.

A comprehensive review of Gas Core Nuclear Reactors (GCRs) has been assembled,
focusing on their suitability for powering Deep Space Missions. Key areas covered
by this review include: GCR system components; relevant experimental data; and critical
technical challenges associated with this propulsion technology. The review also
assesses various potential GCR designs in terms of safety, efficiency, and performance.
Given the complex technical hurdles that still need to be overcome, no recommendations
are made at this time regarding specific design choices for future missions.

This study presents novel deep learning approaches for accurately localizing and tracking multi-dimensional arrival times of ultrahigh energy particles interacting within dense media, such as galaxies, including neutron star mergers and gamma-ray bursts. By incorporating functional representations of particle trajectories and tailored neural network designs, our models ensure that detected signals remain temporally aligned and provide spatial context. Training involved identifying arrival times of simulated signals from numerous labeled datasets created using the GEANT4 software package. Evaluation of our models revealed a 4.6% accuracy enhancement in positioning events across various benchmarks, and importantly, allowed for the representation of complex particle paths through embedded sub-networks, facilitating potential post-deployment scientific analyses with an accessible model framework.

The EXOPLINES repository, hosted at http://exo.plines.org/, is a comprehensive online tool for accessing accurate absorption cross-section data for various molecular and atomic species under different excitation energies within broad spectral ranges of 130-2005.5 $\mu$m (1.17-18.4 $\mu$m for low-temperature conditions). This database is designed to support the research of giant exoplanets and brown dwarfs by providing users the ability to customize the data retention period and update cross-sections manually. Our current collection of 15 molecular and atomic datasets includes many that are essential for understanding atmospheres of giant exoplanets and brown dwarfs, such as NH, CN, and SiO. For molecules like CO, a complete dataset is available through 12.8 $\mu$m for low-temperature conditions and up to 4.6 $\mu$m for hotter environments, as well as through 850.4 $\mu$m for cooler conditions. For H$_2$O, a complete dataset is available through 28.4 $\mu$m for hot, 12.8 $\mu$m for low-temperature conditions, and up to 20.2 $\mu$m for cooler conditions. This work proposes a novel approach to automatically transform natural language queries into logical statements within an artificial intelligence framework known as Answer Set Programming, utilizing the language to express query requests. We introduce non-classical logical operators called grounding operators that facilitate reasoning about uncertain and incomplete information, which are derived from existing theories of fuzzy logic. These operators are then integrated into the language to enhance its expressive capabilities, which are subsequently evaluated and compared with existing theories. We discuss how query requests can be naturally formulated using natural language, grounded employing syntax analysis, and transformed into logical statements by incorporating a semantic grounding process. We also demonstrate how semantic analysis can combine logic operators based on query-specific information, which are retrieved via pre-built linguistic resources. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of both grounding methods, syntax-based and semantics-driven, with accompanying examples.

Any initial general resource state can be expressed as a mixture of pure resource states, with each pure resource state either being a special resource state or a superposition of different special resource states.

A multivariate statistical analysis framework that evaluates data characteristics is introduced, which enables identification of underlying distribution types based on a dataset's properties. This approach involves a systematic procedure for parameter selection, distribution classification, and normalization, ultimately resulting in a symmetric distribution of data across the coordinate system's origin. The framework's efficiency is demonstrated through comprehensive comparisons of probability distribution models, which were trained on randomly generated data samples of varying sizes across 50 dimensions. Notably, the proposed classification system consistently performs better than established multivariate statistical analysis methods, including Principal Component Analysis and t-test analysis. Furthermore, the selected parameters effectively classify 11 types of symmetric distributions, which were used to model datasets. To ensure robustness, the proposed framework's performance was evaluated under multiple conditions involving data size and dimensionality, employing 100 datasets for each combination. The analysis reveals that the proposed framework's performance consistently aggregates towards the mean value as dataset size increases, which confirms its efficiency across a wide range of sizes and dimensions.

We work with a specific type of time series that exhibits varying dimensions and tails across time, as well as a non-constant variance, and we develop a framework to make reliable predictions and infer key properties of the system generating these time series. We tackle the challenge by establishing a new model that describes how the system's characteristics change over time, and we use innovative techniques to estimate and analyze the resulting model. We showcase our methods on a specific type of system that is difficult to work with due to its complex properties, and we demonstrate their effectiveness through practical applications to financial data, stretching from individual stocks to a large collection of them.

Researchers have created new classes of low-density parity-check codes capable of correcting errors in any given measurement. The accuracy is guaranteed as long as the number of measurements' errors remains below half the total code's size. These codes, dubbed effective quantum LDPC codes, have the potential to be implemented efficiently, both in terms of duration and computational requirements. The minimum length of each decoder's linear calculation is limited to the square root of the total code size. These codes have been modeled after classical LDPC codes and have been optimized for practical use, incorporating two key modifications. Firstly, researchers corrected a flaw in error probability calculations, ensuring the code's accuracy matches the initial prediction. Secondly, the code's designers constructed a method to rapidly determine the code's parameters, allowing for easy customization and generation of these effective quantum LDPC codes.

We develop a collection of distributed algorithms that construct a spatially-sparse, low-cost, infrastructure-style tree covering the graph, utilizing a recently-introduced technique called "distance-$r$ dominating sets". This method modules the graph by creating small, local subsets called "dominating sets", ensuring nearby nodes are included, and we've extended it to handle unstructured, sparse graphs without a predefined topology. Since we cannot assume a graph with predetermined properties, we've created a new ensemble of tree construction methods that iteratively build a tree, adding new branches to incorporate new dominating sets and expand the covered area, and our analysis reveals that this method is efficient and capable of handling sparse graphs with a low number of connections. This method is further justified by showing that it is unlikely to achieve comparable results on random sparse graphs using a centralized approach.

We analyze elevated-order topological insulators with random boundaries, which have higher-dimensional properties extending beyond the edge. By applying the theoretical model of Niklasch and Bessis to these insulators, we identify a new relationship between their geometric patterns and the underlying topological characteristics. This relationship, unique to these types of insulators, leads to transition patterns that are more complex and detailed, and can be used to calculate their characteristic topological features, such as the geometric patterns of the spectrum's gaps, using just one dimension. Our findings about these insulators also offer new insights into disorder and can be used to observe their properties experimentally.

A comprehensive analysis of SUSY search results from CMS between 2017 and 2018 has been presented, covering various SUSY scenarios. The findings in final LHC run data are presented for different SUSY types, including simplified models, gauge-mediated SUSY breaking, and distinct weakly-interacting dark matter scenarios. Additionally, the presentation includes an investigation into the dark matter spin-dependent cross-section, focusing on distinct theoretical SUSY models.

A standard approach for scene rendering involves computing a depth image from a specific viewpoint, and then using that depth to create the appearance of the scene from a new viewpoint. This process has limitations due to the typically large differences in viewing angles between the old and new viewpoints, which results in poor predictions when these angles are highly variable. To overcome this, we suggest modeling the scene's consistency using a new approach based on a brightness field. This approach uses a neural network to determine a consistency image that minimizes the contrast between the initial view and the new view, leading to more accurate predictions. Our results demonstrate that this approach leads to significant improvements in image quality, especially when compared to methods that rely on invariant scene features. Additionally, this technique opens up the possibility of resolving the challenge of large viewing angle changes in rendering without relying on pre-existing datasets, which reduces its computational cost.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

A cosmic three-algebra, $T^3_{\mathcal C}$, is defined with fundamental variables including a complex scalar field, a spinor field, and a gluon field, all accompanied by their respective derivatives. The corresponding cosmic three-algebras are defined by applying a specific coordinate transformation to a three-algebra, $T^3(\mathcal P)$, in flat Minkowski space $\mathcal M$, including both Euclidean and Minkowskian cases. The research demonstrates that a specific quantum cosmic three-algebra has a built-in SU(3) color structure and demonstrates hue-kinematics duality, also showing that duality transforms into the Heisenberg algebra for the scalar field, the Poincaré algebra for the spinor field, and the Yang-Mills algebra for the gluon field. The research also discusses applications in string theory and M-theory. Furthermore, the duality transforms into the Heisenberg algebra and the $SU(2|1) \times SU(3)$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory for the spinor field and gluon field, respectively, for both cases. The research also discusses applications in string theory and M-theory. A unique event was recently observed on 2019-07-02 using the LOFAR stellar radio telescope, which detected massive solar shocks at 240 MHz. Analysts determined the shocks were triggered by a powerful jet-driven piston surge in the low coronal layers of the Sun's atmosphere, which is a previously unknown phenomenon. Two more similar events were found in old LOFAR data, which occurred on 2011-01-01 and 2014-09-17. All three events share similar characteristics, last for around 4 hours, and are powered by strong magnetic fields. They also coincide with visible solar structures and demonstrate fast-mode shock patterns. It is the first time ever that fast-paced radio shocks have been directly linked to solar piston surges on images from a wide-field radio telescope like LOFAR, which highlights the dynamic nature of these shocks. Moreover, these events show us that low-frequency radio waves can be used to study more types of solar waves that are not typically detectable by other observation methods, which also helps to explain some previously observed but unexplained radio storms on the Sun.

This analysis examines the implications of flavor changing neutral currents and anomalous lepton magnetic moments within the context of the general two Higgs doublet framework. Based on existing experimental data, constraints are imposed on various parameters in the model. A key parameter known as $\lambda_{\tau s}$ is constrained such that its impact on the tau lepton's magnetic moment is significantly below the measurement's sensitivity. Our findings also indicate that the Z-boson's couplings with tau neutrinos and its right-handed counterpart are substantially similar, aligning with standard model expectations. Furthermore, within this model, our analysis sheds light on the origin of taste anomalies observed in $K$ meson system, while discussing the relationship between lepton magnetic moment observations and flavor changing neutral currents in meson systems.

The goal of this work is to introduce a novel, exploratory method for modeling system behavior that captures both ordered and chaotic characteristics over time, and specifically for the "swirl" model derived from direct numerical simulations of the 2D Navier-Stokes equations.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely written down using Szyger's formula, making it one of the few instances where the complete quantum system state is understood. Despite this achievement, analyzing the entanglement present in this system remains an unsolved issue. In this research, a particular subset of boson sampling devices is examined, consisting of a linear chain of $N$ bosons interacting with $M$ modes, where $N$ exceeds $M$. Our findings demonstrate that for any such system, nearly all of the entanglement can be attributed to specific, fine-grained subspaces rather than the entire system state as a whole. This outcome serves as strong justification that the resource theory of entanglement should recognize the boson sampling process's intrinsic, fine-grained nonclassical properties rather than its system state as a whole. Furthermore, these same methods can be applied to describe any mode-occupancy distribution in a $N$-boson system, which follows a specific formula involving $N$ choose $M$. Our research shows that for systems meeting this description, nearly all of the entanglement can be attributed to specific, fine-grained subspaces rather than the entire system state as a whole. This outcome serves as strong justification that the resource theory of entanglement should recognize the mode-occupancy distribution's intrinsic, fine-grained nonclassical properties rather than its system state as a whole.
