We investigate the consequences of merging fermionic quasiparticles in a
nanoscale system that interacts with local bosonic degrees of freedom. Our
analysis reveals that even with relatively weak interaction, the combined
fermions will undergo an unconventional collapse into a compact state,
given that the surrounding bosons occupy a significantly smaller space.
This phenomenon has significant implications for optical observations, causing a
noticable shift in optical absorption patterns at specific energy levels tied
to the bosonic trapping potential's scale.

The primary objective of this research is to investigate divergence characteristics in the generalized Thompson groups and braided-Thompson groups. Specifically, we have demonstrated the divergence for $G_n^*$, $F_n^*$, $D_n^*$, $T_{\mathfrak{a}}^*$, $\widetilde{T}_{\mathfrak{a}}^*$, $\widetilde{T}_{\mathfrak{b}}^*$, $BD_n^*$, $BD_{\infty}^*$, $\widetilde{BD}_{\infty}^*$, and $\widetilde{BD}_{\mathfrak{a}}^*$. Moreover, our investigation shows that the generalized Thompson groups exhibit uniform finiteness, whereas the braided-Thompson groups possess a finite ascent property.

Although RAG architecture effectively bridges the gap between pre-trained language and vision models, its current implementation limits its ability to deeply engage in conversations by only using past questions to inform its responses. As a result, it struggles to consistently provide accurate answers to follow-up questions, and even when presented with an additional question, it relies solely on the most recent input. To address this, we refine the RAG architecture by introducing a new inquiry-response framework, which incorporates a specialized DPR seeker module, allowing it to successfully parse and process contextual information within question sets, thus generating more precise and comprehensive responses. Extensive comparisons with the original RAG architecture, as well as DPR's document matching approach, confirm that our proposed framework achieves superior performance in both single and multiple question scenarios, as well as improved VQA results.

This study introduces the concept of a logarithmic burden as a particular form of a Hermitian weighted Dirichlet space, and demonstrates that the perturbed polynomials with this weight adhere to a particular asymptotic structure. This understanding is then utilized to analyze the zeros of L-functions in the critical realm, yielding zeros near a fixed, non-real point at an exponential rate, and establishing that the difference between the real part of the initial zero and this fixed point grows linearly with the degree of the L-function.

Despite being widely used, data quality remains a significant concern in crowdsourced summation. To establish reliable method for evaluating summarization quality, we must select accurate human evaluators. We conducted a study to identify and locate skilled summation reviewers on Amazon Mechanical Turk, investigating several approaches that combine qualification tasks to identify top reviewers. Our analysis explores the effectiveness of various configuration combinations in producing high-quality evaluations. Unlike prior studies, we thoroughly examined the skills of multiple reviewer groups, using rigorous qualification tests to ensure consistency. Our findings reveal that recruiter-designed qualifications play a crucial role in evaluating summarization expertise, and we propose new approaches to recruit skilled reviewers for improved summarization performance.

Short sentence retrieval, a critical component of many language models and downstream tasks, can be inefficient due to traditional methods' high computation and storage requirements. This research addresses the retrieval challenge specifically relevant to long texts, known as text-clips, to improve efficiency and comprehension. A novel approach, Token Shift and Selection transformer (TS2-Net), is developed to overcome existing shortcomings. TS2-Net proposes a novel token-level attention mechanism called shift-attention, enabling efficient query and key representation by leveraging positional information. Additionally, TS2-Net incorporates a novel token selection mechanism to condense text-clips into concise, retrievable signatures. Empirical studies demonstrate TS2-Net's superiority in text-clip retrieval, achieving a notable enhancement of 18.0% Rank-1 accuracy and 13.5% Rank-5 accuracy over traditional approaches using a single NVIDIA V100 GPU.

We've found a way a neutral current, beyond the standard model, can affect taste-changing interactions in top quark processes. Although current experiments have limitations, future measurements on $\tau$ decays from $b\rightarrow s$ transitions and top quark production at the LHC and HL-LHC could reveal these interactions.

Directed hybrid random graphs combine ordered triplets with single edges, allowing us to study their asymptotic properties when the ratio of single to tripled edges is non-zero and the number of nodes goes to infinity. We introduce two new methods for investigating this class of graphs, where we analyze both the existing established model and a slightly modified version with altered edge ratios. By examining a specific model where new single edges are added at every step, we gain insight into the general properties of hybrid graphs. Furthermore, we identify specific cases where the ratio of single to tripled edges can be precisely calculated and we establish a local limit theorem for a specific type of hybrid graph, providing information on the asymptotic behavior of the adjacency matrix's eigenvalues.

This research aims to find a machine learning approach that can identify and categorize disturbances in power line transmission by analyzing wireless signals that are prone to such interference. Notably, this problem has been confined to detecting noise in wireless communications, largely due to the lack of a systematic solution to identify disturbances. Existing algorithms have been focused on noise detection, disregarding the classification of disturbances. Moreover, this research introduces a novel dataset that showcases diverse disturbances, further highlighting the need for this classification. By utilizing convolutional neural networks, this research successfully demonstrates the classification of disturbances from wireless signals. To this end, this work examines the effectiveness of CNN models with varying architecture on the classification of disturbances in power line transmission.

In this work, we examine the behaviour of particles governed by a Klein-Gordon equation within a cosmic string spacetime, accompanied by a global space-time displacement. Utilizing a Lagrangian approach, we derive the energy of these particles, taking into account both rotational energy and potential energy. Our analysis reveals that particle energy is influenced by both spatial and temporal displacements, as well as the displacement gradient, in addition to the existing displacement. We observe that for particles at rest, rotational energy dominates potential energy, whereas at high velocities, potential energy surpasses rotational energy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an increase in displacement, displacement gradient, or gravitational potential constant results in a decrease in rotational energy and an increase in potential energy. Conversely, an increase in gravitational potential constant results in an increase in rotational energy and potential energy.

In the context of measure algebra learning theory, which is based on the category of totally bounded measure algebras, the generalization error is analyzed for any given training and test data, when the underlying totally bounded measure algebra is assumed to be locally stationary. A locally stationary system is one where a finite subset of non-measurable elements does not affect the freeness of the algebra. It is demonstrated that if the freeness degree of the algebra's residual part is non-zero, then the measure algebra error is expected to converge to zero as the data set becomes arbitrarily large, provided the data scales appropriately.

The unique behavior of the deep-vision-cases (DVCS) process can be understood by analyzing specific observables that reflect differences in responses due to electromagnetic and strong forces. One such distinguishable force, known as the recoil proton polarization, has the potential to be extensively studied at current and future high-intensity lepton accelerators like Jefferson Lab, Frascati, J-PARC, and CEA/Saclay. By utilizing cutting-edge technology to detect proton polarization with high precision, the DVCS process can be explored in-depth, thereby providing invaluable insights into various aspects, including two-photon scattering, form factors, quark distribution functions, and hadron physics at the sub-nuclear level, as well as testing new theories like QCD in the semi-hard scaling region.

Artificial intelligence has become an integral part of everyday life, encompassing numerous application areas. This study provides a comprehensive theoretical structure for advanced AI systems, grounded in contemporary knowledge and practice. The developed framework is suitable for autonomous AI system design across diverse application domains, including those involving competitive environments.

Our study explores the thermal behavior of a complex superfluid system composed of spin-orbit linked correlated bosons in an optical lattice. This system supports unique quantum phases distinct from standard Bose-Hubbard models. Utilizing a self-consistent mean-field approach, we explore three specific orderings - a uniform superfluid, a supersolid with periodic phase fluctuations, and a superfluid phase with spatially varying phase shifts. We observe significant shifts in the phase shifts at critical temperatures in accordance with the standard Bose-Einstein condensation model. However, the phase shifts exhibit non-linearity at lower temperatures due to the significant interaction strength of the spin-orbit coupled bosons. This is particularly evident in the supersolid phase, where varying wave functions in different hyperfine states cause noticeable distortions. Additionally, we demonstrate that varying optical lattice depth, spin-orbit coupling, and interaction strength between atoms in different states, while keeping total interaction strength constant, can influence the thermal phase shifts. Yet, despite significant strength of interaction between atoms in the same/state, our findings reveal that the system remains resistant to phase mixing.

A group of vertices in a graph forms a clique if all vertices connect to every other vertex. The minimum number of cliques needed to completely encode a given full graph is studied here, using a specific encoding based on subgraph inclusion. For a full encoding, we consider the smallest possible set of cliques from a specific subset $\mathcal{G}$ that includes graphs with 1, 2, 3, and 4 vertices. The minimum number of cliques needed from $\mathcal{G}$ to encode a full graph is known as the graph's $\mathcal{G}$-degeneracy. It is shown that the $\mathcal{G}$-degeneracy can be used to describe the hierarchy of graphs in $\mathcal{G}$ and that the $\mathcal{G}$-degeneracy sequence of graphs in $\mathcal{G}$ with a given number of vertices forms a sequence of non-negative integers. The study of $\mathcal{G}$-degeneracy is developed for finite abelian groups $G$, which includes both the cyclic groups $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and the direct sum of cyclic groups, $p\)-groups, and it is primarily focused on rings and lattices when $G$ has at least two elements. For rings $R$, a measure of ring-degeneracy, $rd(R)$, is defined and used to establish relationships between $rd(R)$, the number of elements

We explore the AdS/CFT correspondence in two and one spatial dimensions with particular emphasis on holographic gauge theories exhibiting supersymmetry. Notably, solutions in one dimension are relatively underexplored; thus, most theoretical frameworks rely on reducing known solutions from higher dimensions, particularly Type IIA with 16 or eight supercharges, as in NS-NS or R-R cases. However, our primary focus lies on solutions with eight supercharges involving a new class of gauged supergravity in AdS$_3$ with a non-Abelian flux, unlike previously studied solutions. Notably, this solution stands out with decoupling and stringy corrections being separable, unlike other known solutions. Furthermore, unlike other known solutions, this solution stands out with decoupling and stringy corrections being separable, with calculable one-loop black hole solutions existing. Additionally, time-dependent solutions in AdS$_1$ are found using a new approach, with calculable one-loop contributions found for conical solutions with eight supercharges, in contrast to previously existing solutions without such contributions.

This work offers an undergraduate mathematics curriculum that utilizes fundamental mathematical expressions to create Gaussian process kernel formulations. These standardized formulations provide a unified framework that accommodates various kernels previously presented in literature, thereby serving as a concise reference for reproduction and replication. The approach is further illustrated by applying it to four established Gaussian Process regression techniques. Additionally, this study examines the computational efficiency of the proposed methodology, demonstrating that its scalability is suited for applications on typical workstations.

The forthcoming muon colliders will likely be limited by beam-induced background effects. Several innovative schemes have been proposed to reduce these effects in hadron colliders, which could serve as a model for future lepton colliders. This paper examines and compares four concepts for decreasing beam-induced background at muon colliders, focusing on strategies to separate and separate the beam and its decay products in time, space, and phase space. The outcomes are promising, suggesting it's feasible to reduce final focus design constraints by up to two orders of magnitude and decrease beam-induced background effects to a level where background processes become detectable on top of the signal.

Introducing Spartan, an innovative approach for training neural networks with predefined sparsity. This method involves leveraging a previously developed criterion for statistical sparsity and employing a novel, weighted transportation algorithm based on GANs. Unlike other neural network sparsification methods, Spartan exceeds 90% edge sparsity in real-world tasks like language modeling and text generation, while also outperforming state-of-the-art methods in reconstructive sparsity. Moreover, Spartan maintains the capacity for gradient-based training, thereby allowing for efficient backpropagation and easy integration with existing neural network frameworks. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of Spartan, including its theoretical underpinnings, evaluation protocol, and empirical evaluation of its performance.

According to theories based on Weyl semimetals and Majorana modes, an emergent Pauli obstruction requires the Bloch frame of a system's momentum space to have a Z2 anomaly, meaning that the orientation of the frame cannot be consistently defined across the entire momentum space.  However, researchers have now challenged this idea by demonstrating through density-matrix renormalization group simulations that an emergent Pauli obstruction does indeed exist in a weakly interacting Bose fluid.  This was achieved by generating a strength of interaction that acts like a spin-orbit coupling, resulting in the anomaly.  Furthermore, both enclosed momentum loops and helical bound states of the system's edges have been found to exhibit Z2 obstruction, which is defined as non-trivial topological invariant in the system's bulk.  This finding has significant implications, showing that the anomalous system's bulk is inscribed in a topologically non-trivial band, resulting in the non-enclosed momentum loop's properties.

Previous studies indicated developers may avoid discussing software issues due to perceived embarrassment or fear of being dismissed. A survey of 101 Java developers revealed 42% had encountered situations where they avoided discussing issues, with 20% experiencing multiple such instances. Empirical analysis of chat platforms and code review tools supported the hypothesis that developers often refrain from discussing certain issues. The survey results also showed that most developers consider "test failures" a serious issue, with 66% labeling it as very or extremely serious. Conversely, developers viewed "loose codes" as less serious, with 33% labeling it as very or extremely serious. Notably, there was a discrepancy between the developers' perception of issue seriousness and their willingness to discuss it, suggesting developers may still avoid discussing "loose codes" despite perceiving it as a relatively minor issue.

This paper investigates the resolution of optimality conditions for a problem that involves a nonconvex sweeping process over a set that is Lipschitz. The dynamics of the problem are described by a differential equation that incorporates an integral term, with optimality conditions derived through the use of subdifferentials. The result is an innovative method that enables the evolution of the problem to be fully utilized in the calculation of the subdifferential, even when the problem is nonconvex. Several case studies, including a problem of optimal control with mixed state and control constraints, confirm the potential of the new sweeping surface.

We introduce a new version of the KKMCee event generator, specifically designed for creating lepton and quark pairs in lepton collider events through the various underlying fundamental interactions. In this context, 'ee' denotes even even final states consisting of specific particle number configurations in leptons and quarks, which will be used extensively in future lepton collider experiments to achieve precise particle mass measurements. To accomplish this goal, we have incorporated the multi-photon Monte Carlo event generator in KKMCee, enabling the event generator to model 'ee' processes involving unpaired photons, which represents a crucial breakthrough for creating realistic 'ee' events. Furthermore, we have utilized unpaired photons to establish even odd event scenarios in addition to 'ee' events. We have verified the reliability of this new event generator by conducting in-depth comparisons with PHOTOS. We have also provided concrete, real-world examples of 'ee' events influenced by specific polarized photon decay methods, which could be utilized in future lepton collider experiments to promote the development of polarized photon decay simulations.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals is crucial for heart health because even minor changes can indicate chronic or acute cardiovascular issues. However, signal noise and the diverse ranges of inter-beat intervals make them challenging to analyze. We developed a novel approach using the Tiramisu framework to assess inter-beat intervals, which combines captureNet for data preprocessing and attentionUNet for classification. Our approach successfully identifies inter-beat intervals with exceptional accuracy, surpassing current standards by a significant margin with a 4% error rate.

The nonnegative least squares problem for the tensor factorization of n-dimensional arrays has been proven to be a reliable method for calculating the low-rank tensor approximation with the least error in a noisy array. In order to expedite the calculation, we developed an iterative algorithm that alternates between random walks in the nonnegative least squares problem and a tensor factorization update. The algorithm is analogous to the stochastic gradient descent approach but incorporates passes through the entire data set to enhance convergence performance. The method is similar to the alternating least squares algorithm, but our approach accelerates convergence by bypassing detailed calculations for each factor matrix. The algorithm's effectiveness was validated using datasets of small and moderate size, and also in comparative studies which showed that it converges faster or at least equally well as other methods, while utilizing fewer operations. Furthermore, we applied the algorithm to the calculation of the low-rank tensor approximation with the least error in a noisy array, and obtained results that match the accuracy of the calculation obtained with the calculation of the tensor singular value decomposition.

Network embedding techniques that use learning to represent graph components in a lower-dimensional space have gained significant traction in various applications. However, the field of embedding dynamic networks, which consist of rapidly changing nodes and edges, remains underdeveloped due to the absence of suitable frameworks and methods. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach called EvoLink that targets the embedding of nodes in evolving graphs, focusing on retaining crucial structural information. To achieve this, EvoLink incorporates two key components: a framework that combines community and rich club maximization to capture the core graph structure and a novel approach using Temporal Autoencoder for edge prediction, allowing the capture of temporal information in evolving networks. Additionally, EvoLink incorporates a strategy to preserve temporal edge information. Experimental evaluations using synthetic and real-world datasets showcase the superiority of EvoLink in capturing both temporal and structural properties by comparing it with existing methods using edge prediction, graph visualization, and information retrieval metrics. Notably, EvoLink demonstrates improved performance using reduced dimensions and faster processing times compared to the state-of-the-art approach by Google's Graph Neural Network (GNN).

Theoretical research has made significant progress in studying deuterium's isospin partners, particularly positron emission, which includes the study of deuterium's analogs with s-wave resonances. One such resonance, the $^7$H base state, has been identified as a $^3$H+4n combination and calculated to have a mass of approximately 8.053 039 82 MeV, with a width of 0.000 035 83 MeV, in accordance with recent experimental findings.

In this paper, we investigate a variant of Nirenberg's problem for completing the metric on $S^{2n+1} \# k\mathbb{R}^2$ and we demonstrate that for most values of k, this completion does not arise from a blowup of the compact eigenvalues. However, we also show that for k being either 1 or 3, this completion does arise from a blowup of the compact eigenvalues.

Our approach presents a novel method for adapting self-supervised visual representation learning that leverages contrastive learning with the Sinkhorn distance. This distance allows us to effectively apply the Triplet of Triangles loss, a measure of similarity that offers several advantages, including scalability, caucus property, and a clear separation between classes. The results of our comprehensive experiments conducted on large, real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach, as it outperforms existing self-supervised methods by a significant margin. The strength of our method lies in its ability to generate high-quality representations that surpass those produced by supervised learning in our tests on multiple classification tasks. The exceptional performance of our approach is due to two key factors. Firstly, the Triplet of Triangles loss tends to group similar images into nearest neighbor groups that are more sparse than those created by existing contrastive learning methods. Secondly, our approach is able to achieve a substantial reduction in computational complexity by leveraging the properties of the Sinkhorn distance that make it easier to scale up to large datasets. The results of our experiments confirm that our method for efficient self-supervised visual representation learning is unparalleled in the field.

In 2020, contact tracing for COVID-19 became a critical public health tool for managing outbreaks, minimizing infections, hospitalizations, and mortality worldwide. Contact tracing programs relied heavily on contact tracing data, which were analyzed to identify potential transmission links. This research focuses on the role of regional tracing collaborations in contact tracing and pandemic management. Using stochastic petri networks, the law of large numbers is applied to model COVID-19 spread and contact tracing for a population divided into regions, each with its own contact tracing capabilities. This approach is grounded in real-world data from England's COVID-19 outbreak. Through simulation and statistical inference, regional tracing collaborations are shown to enhance average isolation and quarantine periods, which lead to decreased pandemic severity and length. Specifically, our findings demonstrate that regional collaborations can shorten the pandemic's duration by 10% to 20% and decrease the cumulative number of infections by up to 25%. This study utilizes COVID-19 data in England but offers insights into managing outbreaks with regional tracing collaborations for infectious diseases.

Determining a universal correction factor for distance predictions based on Gaia TRVs remains a pressing challenge. To address this issue, researchers created a comprehensive dataset of binary stars within Melotte 72 using the Gaia DR2 survey. A statistical approach was employed to derive kinematic parameters for 60 stars in the cluster. Next, authors applied various methods to identify binaries, selecting those with up to 20:1 period ratios. Following this, researchers classified the binaries and differentiated first-order systems from higher-order ones. Consequently, 44 primary binaries were selected for the study. To derive cluster parameters, authors used seven distinct methods, including parameters from kinematics and binary systems. Notably, when binaries were excluded, researchers found that Gaia TRVs yielded a 4% root mean square error, while kinematic parallaxes revealed a 19% root mean square error. Moreover, parallax distributions across multiple analysis methods aligned closely, with a cross-correlation of at least 85%. These results suggested that Gaia DR2 underestimates parallaxes by 15%. Furthermore, authors found that the cluster clocked in at a rate of $${\rm dyr}=(7.755\pm 0.064)$$ with a age of $(5.488\pm 0.322)$ million years. Lastly, authors found the cluster possessed a solar equivalent radius of $(7.017\pm 0.998)\, {\rm pc}$$, with a

We're exploring Betti numbers in the context of Gaussian processes on the sparse domain. Building on work by Ollivier-Rudelson and Buhler-O'Donnell in sample spaces defined by $\chi_{p,n}$, we establish analogous results for the sparse domain $\lambda_{p,n}$. By leveraging our findings for the sparse domain, we achieve a more significant extension than what Ollivier-Rudelson offered, as our work allows for any $0 < p \leq \infty$. Furthermore, we establish a new correlation bound in the sample space defined by $\lambda_{p,n}$ with $0 < p \leq \infty$.

In robotics, adjusting an eye-in-hand camera involves moving the camera while attached to a robot arm to capture a clear image of an object. However, capturing a single image does not provide information on the camera's position or orientation. This research presents an innovative method for calculating a 6-dimensional pose from a single image by employing a pre-generated point cloud as a reference. To account for variations in object texture, a density map is used in conjunction with the object's depth map to define the pose optimization problem. To solve this problem, the algorithm starts by estimating the object's depth from the initial camera position. To improve the solution's accuracy, the object's depth is refined in a sequence of iterations, with the camera adjusting itself in each iteration to better match the generated density map. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our algorithm can efficiently calculate the 6-dimensional pose from a single image, even when the object appears in poorly textured scenarios.

Our focus with inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) is to deduce a target reward function from a set of observed expert trajectories. Although IRL has been extensively researched in the context of static environments, little is known about how to apply this concept to dynamic environments following the multi-agent reinforcement learning framework. Essentially, we are trying to determine how to translate differing agent evaluation metrics into a unified framework. To address this, we introduce a novel IRL approach for real-time dynamic multi-agent environments without the need for prior knowledge or hand-designed features. Our method, featuring an entropy regularized actor-policy training approach, achieves the lowest known sample complexity in the one-step look-ahead markov decision process. Additionally, we leverage the diversity of initial evaluation outputs to learn the optimal target reward function, resulting in consistent improvements. Our experiments showcase the effectiveness of this approach in a range of situations.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission, a precision space observatory, is dedicated to creating a detailed 3D map of the galaxy's stellar content with unprecedented accuracy and scale, which will be the largest dataset ever generated, spanning 1 billion sources. However, the mission's vast array of data and complex analysis process necessitate cutting-edge IT systems to process and analyze the data in real-time. Although the mission's scope is vast, the article will specifically focus on the challenges and opportunities related to creating the 3D map of the galaxy's stellar content.

To find the minimum treewidth of a large graph, we typically use vertex separators, but these often use an excessive number of vertices, leading to a space complexity issue. To mitigate this problem, we've developed a new approach that employs vertex separators with a guaranteed minimum size, significantly improving the space efficiency. In our experiments, this technique has resulted in a substantial improvement in space usage for graph structures, with an average reduction of 50% observed. We've also demonstrated the practical applicability of this method by integrating it with a maximum-weight partitioning algorithm, achieving a notable speedup of treewidth computation in real-world datasets.

Network analysis through the lens of community structure provides valuable insights, albeit with community representation concerns. The development of community structure methods tailored to incorporate varying node importance and directional relationships in weighted networks offers a solution. This paper delves into the implications of incorporating node importance and allow negative edge weights, further outlining the requirements for applying these approaches to inferred and assessed networks.

Complex simulations frequently rely on machine learning models, especially in sciences where small inaccuracies in biophysical or medical models can have severe health implications, prompting a need for formal validation processes.  Currently, validating these models is an intricate and costly process, involving data collection and analysis.  An alternative approach, demonstrated in this study through an example involving a physical neural network, is a posteriori evaluation that relies on empirical evidence from the model's behavior.  This new approach, an extension of traditional concepts including leverage theory and influence function, is an essential tool for ensuring high-accuracy predictions, especially in high-stakes applications involving physics-based machine learning models.

Epidemiological research utilizes geostatistical techniques and machine learning methods to investigate various environmental factors influencing health outcomes worldwide. This study focuses on utilizing geospatial data and artificial intelligence techniques to analyze and model air pollution, air temperature, and rainfall patterns to understand their impact on outdoor activities and gather insights into COVID-19 spread across the Brazilian national territory. We employed artificial neural networks, trained with data from weather stations located across Brazil, to predict two-hour air temperature and pollution patterns over unobserved areas. These predictions were then utilized in an extensive analysis of COVID-19 confirmed cases and deaths, along with other environmental and socioeconomic factors, through spatial regression modeling. The findings indicate that high air pollution levels, particularly when pollution levels exceed 50 $\mu$m$^{-1}$, are associated with increased COVID-19 case and fatality rates, whereas low air temperature and intense rainfall periods also correlate with higher case and fatality rates, although with lesser significance than air pollution. These results stress the importance of atmospheric quality in public health, emphasizing the need for efficient policies to minimize the risks associated with exposure to polluted urban atmospheres.

A major challenge in developing topological superconducting systems revolves around identifying the Majorana zero mode (MZ) through the appearance of a zero-bias peak (ZBP) in tunneling spectra. However, the presence of ZBP is not exclusive to the MZ, as it can arise from various other phenomena such as vortices and Andreev resonators. To separate the MZ from these competing ZP's, we present a theory based on tunneling spectroscopy utilizing resistive electrodes. The introduction of ohmic dissipation in the system simplifies the electronic density of states around vortices and reveals distinct characteristics distinct from the MZ. Furthermore, the presence of resistive electrodes enables the utilization of a comparative analysis of ZP's from different leads, ultimately revealing unique signatures of the MZ. Additionally, we discuss how the proposed technique can be applied to recognize multiple ZP's generated by Andreev resonators.

Theoretical foundations of linear bandits, an unsupervised learning paradigm, have remained underdeveloped in comparison to their supervised counterparts. This study provides a comprehensive statistical analysis of a modified version of the "where the action is" linear bandit problem with heterogeneous action sets, initially proposed by Gai and Xu (2012). In contrast to their work, which focused on a Bayesian approach, our investigation utilizes a frequentist framework. We derive the first frequentist analysis of the problem, establishing the frequentist analysis for the first time. Additionally, our study offers important practical implications, as the action estimates obtained through our method can be directly applied in a real-time Bayesian switching linear bandit model without requiring any adjustments to the Bayesian model. Our theoretical findings are supported by complementary simulation studies.

Researchers introduced the concept of orbital Hall effect as an alternative to valley-polarized conductance in graphene with a gap. By applying a gate voltage, they create a pattern of charge density within the sample that exhibits a specific orbital configuration, resulting in a local magnetic moment. Due to this magnetic moment, they predict that the orbital arrangement will influence the flow of current, displaying a type of orbital Hall effect. A specific type of orbital configuration in graphene, with two distinct pockets, can mimic the behavior of two valleys, demonstrating equivalent Hall resistance and transmission rates. A probe using a single incoming electron can display different responses, depending on which orbital is being sampled, while showing near identical responses to being in a valley or another orbital configuration. This new type of orbital Hall effect is an innovative way to study the properties of graphene, offering a range of applications in medical and optical transport devices.

Stochastic graph neural networks have seen extensive adoption due to their capacity to model uncertain geometric data. However, current implementations lack a solution for handling graph data corruption that occurs in real-world scenarios, where inaccurate results may lead to decision-making in high-stakes environments. To bridge this gap, our research introduces a method for simulating graph data corruption and a subsequent RL approach for optimizing GNN parameters to combat it. The proposed Q-learning strategy adapts GNNs to perform well under both known and unknown corruption scenarios. Experimental evaluations utilizing various GNN types and multiple types of corruption confirm the efficacy of our approach, and show that it surpasses traditional training methods in performance when faced with corruption and outperforms a baseline Q-learning variant that doesn't account for noise.

The process of aligning surveys relies on accurate mapping to minimize measurement errors, which can be achieved by transforming datasets. Although the process typically utilizes astrometry, photometric data can also be applied and combined to facilitate a more accurate and robust alignment. This study examines and tests the pros and cons of utilizing photometric data in conjunction with astrometry for survey alignment, with the aim of determining key findings and recommendations for survey mapping. By developing and implementing a generic algorithm to combine multiple astrometry and photometric measurements, the results revealed that the photometric data contributes to an improved alignment with minimal empirical offsets, which is particularly evident in regions with high levels of astrometric uncertainty. This finding is confirmed through the analysis of two real-world surveys, namely the Euclid Survey and the Legacy Survey of Space and Time. Based on the findings, the photometric and astrometric data can be combined to achieve a more accurate alignment with minimal empirical offsets, which is particularly beneficial for surveys with low-to-moderate levels of astrometric uncertainty. Furthermore, the photometric data is the most influential when the astrometric uncertainty is very low, which is the standard for future surveys such as Euclid and LSST.

In this paper, we investigate the topological properties of infinite hypergraphs and their corresponding minimal vertex sets. A hypergraph is deemed $k$-Sipserian when every minimal vertex subset of size at least $k$ contains a subset of size $k$ that, in turn, has a complete intersection in the hypergraph. The largest possible size of a $k$-Sipserian hypergraph for a given number of vertices is denoted by $\pi_k(n)$ and is determined recursively. Specifically, for a given $k$-Sipserian hypergraph with $\ell$ vertices, the next largest size $\ell+1$ can be calculated as the maximum of two expressions involving sums and products of previous values of the hypergraph for smaller or equal $\ell$ values. By establishing a recursive formula for the hypergraph, we are able to find a recursive definition of the sequence $\pi_k(n)$ and show that for a given $k$, the sequence $\pi_k(n)$ grows at least as $\Omega(\frac{n}{\log^n p})$ and at most as $\frac{n}{\log^{k-1} 2n}$ for $n$ vertices, where $0<p<1$. A similar growth is observed for the number of edges in the optimal hypergraph for a given number of vertices $n$ and size $m$. Moreover, we find that for a given number of vertices $n$, the largest possible size

This paper introduces an innovative visual representation, or plot, called OntoPlot. Designed for hierarchical domains, OntoPlot accommodates non-hierarchical relationships within a minimized display area. A fishbone layout, incorporating radial and linear elements, distinguishes parent from child components. An innovative radial layout in OntoPlot prevents visual clutter and fusion of components even in dense data sets, preserving hierarchical structures and reducing visual complexity. For non-hierarchical relationships, OntoPlot utilizes an innovative off-radial layout that prevents visual noise and fusion and makes it easier to focus on essential information. By merging these two types of data into a single visual representation, OntoPlot distinguishes and emphasizes hierarchical and non-hierarchical relationships without adding to the overall visual display area. Through user testing and case studies involving domain experts, it has been demonstrated that OntoPlot's visual representations, including integrated and isolated views of hierarchical and non-hierarchical data, aid users in data analysis and understanding. Furthermore, it has been found that OntoPlot's radial layout visualizations enhance data exploration and understanding, while OntoPlot's integrated visualizations facilitate various data analysis tasks.

Automated Speech Transcription is a complex task requiring large amounts of speech-data paired with transcripts. We explore a novel semi-supervised approach to reduce reliance on extensive annotated data, leveraging unsupervised end-to-end models to eliminate the need for paired training sets. To this end, we develop a training objective incorporating two penalties: a cycle consistency penalty to improve unsupervised representations and an inter-domain penalty to bridge the gap between speech and text domains. Experimental results on the WMZ corpus indicate that this approach compares favorably to existing methods, with the inter-domain penalty appearing particularly crucial for improving unsupervised representations.

A pioneering approach known as Procedural Knowledge Media (PKM), developed by Dr. Robert Meersman in the late 20th century, aimed to create more realistic artificial intelligence systems. Unlike traditional data-driven methods, PKM-based AI systems, like those built using rules and object-oriented programming, can exhibit human-like behavior through their dynamic and evolutionary nature. This paper proposes a novel method, Profound Active Deduction (PAD), which enables a PKM-based AI system to model human thought processes more accurately. Building on a revised understanding of human reasoning as a dynamic and iterative process, PAD incorporates concepts from epistemology and dynamics to create a framework for simulating and understanding both implicit and explicit human thinking patterns. Furthermore, PAD has been successfully used to explain human decision-making and behavior through its ability to model derived concepts and evaluate their dynamics. This paper also showcases an integrated PAD-based robotic navigation system, where a human-like AI system automatically generates and adapts its own strategies and policies in response to various environmental and task-specific factors. This developed system, featuring a complex robotic task, has been compared against human navigation and robot navigation data to verify its effectiveness and relevance.

The Soret effect, which describes the separation of a substance under temperature gradients, has been explored in terms of the role played by flexible molecules. Our investigation focuses on the Soret coefficient as a measure of thermal diffusion in solutions formed from chemically inert, flexible molecules. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we examined Soret coefficients for various models of polymer-like molecules, including both non-polar and polar variants, in different liquid solvents that were also flexible. We discovered that the Soret coefficients of non-polar molecules exhibit significant sensitivity to temperature gradients when the molecules are relatively non-polarized, but only show a significant response to gradients when the molecules are polarized when the molecules are polarized. The Soret coefficients of polar molecules, on the other hand, demonstrate a range of responses to temperature gradients, but this behavior is found to be largely independent of the degree of internal flexibility exhibited by the molecules. The explanations for these findings are rooted in the interplay between internal flexibility, molecular shape, and intermolecular interactions, such that stiffer molecular segments are able to form more stable intermolecular interactions that are sensitive to temperature gradients, resulting in increased thermal diffusion, but that conformational changes due to internal flexibility serve to weaken this trend in the case of polar molecules.

In the realm of music aesthetics, numerous composition evaluation methods have been developed over the years. The advent of large-scale language models based on transformer architecture has led to breakthroughs in music generation, as well as innovations in evaluating generated music. This study employs a transformer-based language model to evaluate musical compositions by analyzing how they conform to underlying expectations in the data. These expectations are implicitly derived from a corpus of normal music patterns. The proposed method demonstrates the capacity for a language model to serve as a music critic, providing valuable guidance for composers to refine their craft. Experimental results and qualitative analyses are presented to illustrate the capabilities of this novel approach.

In recent years, domain adaptive pedestrian detection methods have garnered significant attention for minimizing the need for costly pixel-level data annotation. However, these methods primarily focus on addressing domain discrepancies between the training and testing datasets, overlooking the fact that a given training image may contain multiple unrelated scenes. This phenomenon is known as intra-domain variability. As a result, training models using a dataset with multiple sub-domains (e.g. different cities) can lead to false positives and impede generalization. To address this issue, this study introduces a novel unsupervised approach that reduces false positives and adapts to domain differences simultaneously. The core idea is to reorder the bounding boxes in a way that clusters individuals and isolates irrelevant areas. This is achieved by learning a shared space for feature representation and box ordering through an efficient rank loss function. The proposed method boasts a computational complexity that is linear rather than quadratic, making it suitable for large datasets. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, yielding a 78.7% reduction in false positives and improved adapted performance on pedestrian re-identification and domain adaptive pedestrian detection tasks.

This paper reveals how leveraging knowledge from the visual world can significantly impact music education. By exploring the potential of computer vision in music instruction, we investigate the differences between system-designed and human-made patterns of variation in image-based learning. Furthermore, we propose novel network architectures for improving both small-scale and large-scale music collections, utilising insights from the way the human brain processes images and auditory information. Building upon these findings, we develop cutting-edge methods for transforming music using multiple types of data and demonstrate that these algorithms can be used to create new musical compositions.

In this research, we introduce FauxThrow, a realistic throwing task where users are asked to release the ball at an incorrect point, leading to an automatic calculation of the necessary throwing force to make the ball land in the target area. Through both experimental studies with 21 participants and virtual environment studies with 18 participants, we discovered that users who used an incorrect release point struggled to achieve the target, with most struggles occurring when the target's height differs from the released ball's height. Our research also reveals that users do not adequately utilize available vertical space when the target's height is higher than the released ball's height or insufficient vertical space exists when the target's height is lower than the released ball's height. With the assistance of our designed FauxThrow protocol, this study successfully simulates and evaluates users' throwing abilities under these constraints in a controlled manner for the first time.

This paper presents an innovative interpretation module that couples a neural machine translation model, enhancing its ability to explain the translation process by providing syntactic breakdowns. Built on an analysis of translation habits, the system builds upon an existing tree structure built during translation, utilizing it to generate targeted syntactic segments that mirror the tree's structure. A novel top-to-bottom decoding method is employed to facilitate this process, enabling faster convergence and more precise matches between tree nodes and individual syntactic segments. To promote more accurate parsing, a new type of neural link is introduced between trees nodes and words, enabling the model to learn preferred connections during training. Experimental results on the IWSLT 2006 English-to-Russian dataset demonstrate that the new interpretation module achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, parsing 59.9% of sentences accurately, a significant improvement over the 52.7% achieved by previous research. Additionally, the entire translation corpus was manually evaluated to further validate the model's performance, confirming our findings.

In order to determine the most crucial molecules to experiment with at scale, our free, open-source 'BEAP' platform analyzes the stability of molecules based on theoretical models and the availability of reactants in space. BEAP assesses a molecule's ability to form given the environmental conditions, taking into account the relative amounts of reactants, the likelihood of collisions, and other factors. BEAP's algorithm relies on accurate binding energy data, so we've developed a database of theoretical binding energies for molecules and pairs of atoms to ensure consistency. By comparing the formation energies of molecules and pairs of atoms, BEAP identifies the most favorable species in a given environment. Based on a panel of expert judgments, our study shows that these predictions are accurate in nearly 85% of cases. To ensure these predictions remain reliable, our database of binding energies will be continuously updated with new entries. By providing access to this database, BEAP's predictions can be used to develop targeted experimental efforts to validate or refine molecular structures and help scientists better understand the complex chemical environment of space. All of the platform's code and binding energy data can be accessed without charge at beap.org.

A multiplicative stochastic model with a sample-dependent lower bound is proposed and its key characteristics are identified. The proposed model has applications in finance, specifically in modeling long-term stock price bottoms sampled at distinct times. The model's implementation involves using one data point to establish a parameter, after which it can be employed for the analysis of price bottoms using least squares. The model's parameters can also be determined via stochastic backward induction, which requires the execution of a particle swarm algorithm due to the sample-dependent nature of the model, resulting in a deterministic outcome. The model's performance and that of the traditional Bell-Allen model are compared through numerical analysis, revealing that the proposed model yields more accurate results when analyzing stationary price trends, however, it tends to overestimate when compared to the Bell-Allen model which assumes price non-stationarity. The proposed model has several benefits over its counterpart as it offers explanatory power, allows for the analysis of price trends in the long and short term, and can also be used as a price forecasting tool, demonstrating this through both theoretical and practical case studies.

Deep learning techniques using activation functions based on threshold response have
seen substantial success in activation-based circuit simulations, but their
applications in experimental settings are limited due to requirements for high
circuit depth and low error rates. This article presents shallow shades, a method
using low-error rate deep circuits and employing threshold response for each qubit
state projection, resulting in a significant decrease in required depth, achieving
a low average error rate of 0.75 percent with only three levels of rotation. The
outcome shows shallow shades outperforming deep and low-error rate circuits in
experimental applications, with an example use case showcasing its superiority
over shallow circuits in boson sampling. With shadowns showing potential in this
area, our study provides the first known application of threshold response in
quantum information processing. The implementation of this concept in real
experimental settings is a first, making these results highly applicable in
real-world scenarios.

For the reflection and outgoing coefficients in the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we've found a significant $|k|$ behavior, where $k$ represents wavenumber in a two-dimensional setting with waves propagating in both two and one directions. We used this behavior to verify an inverse scattering result for a broader class of equations than previously considered. Additionally, we demonstrated the possibility of solitons interacting and merging, and we discussed how superposition of multiple solutions can result in unique solutions that don't arise from the combination of individual entries.

To enhance the resilience of text classification models, we introduce a method for generating diverse yet accurate labeling variants by utilizing existing labels and labels within specified ranges. This approach is inspired by language's inherent variability and our observation that standard label variations (e.g. "yes" vs. "yes indeed") are often underutilized in current frameworks. A novel labeling model, referred to as Sibyl, is developed to create a multitude of labels for training, effectively mitigating catastrophic data acquisition scenarios such as data poisoning and distribution shift. Importantly, our method achieves high performance without sacrificing it on the original task. Through extensive experiments with various scenarios, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in creating resilient variants.

Currently available techniques for developing convolutional neural networks from
scratch on drawing and painting data fall short, resulting in low accuracy.
Conventional fine-tuning and "brush-replay" methods can effectively leverage
small-scale datasets but become impractical with larger datasets. In response,
we are introducing an innovative meta-learning framework that met its goals in
real-world testing. This framework, built upon a unique neuron design, allows
for efficient learning, adaptable stroke policies, and optimized coloration
without any need for comprehensive stroke optimization. Furthermore, our
analysis reveals that our stroke policy generates effective, coherent, and
realistic movements that can be manipulated across different scales.

Knowledge distillation has become a preferred method for creating smaller language models that are cheaper to train and run. However, its performance in resource-scarce machine translation (MT) for languages like Nepali, especially when neural machine translation has limited adaptability to low-resource languages, poses significant challenges. This study assesses the reliability of distillation in creating a lightweight MT model for Nepali, comparing it with quantization, and also investigates the impact of different training techniques, including using teacher models of varying capacities, utilizing data augmentation methods like text reordering to improve the performance in our experiments. The results show that, distillation leads to better performance than quantization, and using a larger teacher model yields more reliable outcomes than using a basic one, and incorporating data augmentation techniques leads to more consistent results than not using them.

Consider a hypergraph with edge $E$ and vertices $V$. Assume $a$ instances of each unique vertex in $V$ are included in $E$. Define a function $f(E)$ as the product of these $a$ values, representing the copy count of each $V$ vertex in $E$. This gives us a non-negative function, where a product of zeros equals zero and a product of non-zeroes is also zero. The properties of $f(E)$ include being invariant to the addition or removal of a single element, the permutation of elements, and the inclusion of additional elements whose values would result in zero. This makes $f(E)$ useful for determining the solvability of equations of a specific type, specifically hypergraph isomorphism problems where two given graphs have the same structure but different labels for their vertices and edges. This approach can also solve equations where a number of identical terms are equal to a specific non-zero value, confirming an existing theorem regarding the irreducibility of a certain type of function and expanding upon it by describing the partitions of a given number where each element is a non-zero value, represented by the product of those number's divisors.

To accelerate research in pneumonia segmentation, we investigated whether image processing techniques could reduce the reliance on extensive labeled datasets. Given that current segmentation methods focus on distinct pulmonary patterns, we developed methods to emphasize desired features and diminish irrelevant details. Three image enhancement methods were employed: Unsharp Mask, for distinguishing pulmonary patterns against the background; Sobel operators, for highlighting detailed structural elements; and Adaptive Equalization, for optimizing pixel intensity and enhancing the visibility of pattern characteristics. We applied these methods to four datasets with a varied degree of success and found that the smallest set, originally requiring extensive annotation, became accessible without significant labeling by experts. Furthermore, the best outcomes were achieved using a combination of the Unsharp Mask and Adaptive Equalization methods in conjunction with a pre-trained U-Net model, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach.

Deep neural network-based image captioning embodies a key challenge as a semi-supervised learning task: generating descriptive text from images. However, conventional techniques typically involve lengthy training times and substantial annotated datasets. To mitigate these challenges, we propose an innovative solution: omitting the necessity for extensive image data and labels through the use of manageable descriptions. Manageable descriptions emphasize concise, easy-to-understand language, enabling users to easily produce and fine-tune them with minimal manual effort. Our approach addresses this issue by employing a few chosen descriptions as training data and leveraging them to refine pre-trained language models' performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our description-based task prompt on the COCO and Flickr30k datasets, showcasing superior image captioning results. Moreover, our approach allows for the production of distinct captioning paradigms such as abstractness, figurative language, and semantic adherence, all starting from a single set of description templates.

Using a conceptual framework, this work delves into the mechanics of damage in systems, focusing on the interplay between internal and external factors that drive deterioration. A broad damage model is proposed and then narrowed down to examine its causal effects in two key contexts: first, looking at how damage caused to a system affects its components, and second, exploring the converse relationship where system-level issues arise from internal or external elements. Building on this, a workbench is developed to test these causal connections, incorporating a simplified model of a toy's mechanical components.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Python 3x and Java/Machine Learning platforms through Spark integration. By leveraging this bridge, developers can seamlessly harness the power of Python 3x deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow, Keras, and Scikit-Learn, while utilizing the vast resources of the Hadoop ecosystem. To demonstrate its capabilities, we will show step-by-step adaptation and scaling of a basic example, illustrating the advantages of this hybrid approach.

We present an approach to translate spoken input into a choice of formal languages, leveraging annotated visual diagrams to facilitate understanding. By combining effective speech recognition, a novel tree-to-tree transfer method, and user-defined symbol mappings, we enable voice commands to be seamlessly encoded into semantic representations. To illustrate the potential of this framework, we show examples of zero-shot voice command inputs translated into logical expressions and LaTeX syntax.

This work introduces a novel type of partial differential inequality, framed as an inequality for the vanishing mean oscillation of a function, and explores its connections with classical heat equation theory. Building upon this, the paper derives universal active boundary conditions for the heat equation, providing a unique solution to the classic heat equation under certain specified boundary conditions. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the relationship between this new inequality and a specific type of functional inequality originally proposed by Payne and Raiti.

Final consumer load data, currently unaccessible, is the last link in the load forecasting chain. This study employs a statistical model combining load forecasts made by consumers with energy experts to create an accurate probabilistic forecast. We analyze the benefits and drawbacks of model selection, combining forecasts, and consider the uncertainty associated with daily peak consumption. Ultimately, we present our model and test it using actual low voltage load data from Dutch consumers.

Deep learning's impressive advancements have led to impressive results across various domain-specific applications. Nevertheless, heavy reliance on large-scale, generalized data leading to 'island effects' often hinders desired outcomes in specialized areas. This limitation can be mitigated by integrating domain expertise into machine learning models for optimized performance. This research outlines a framework for implementation, focusing on embedding domain knowledge using constraint optimization and uncertainty analysis to assess model reliability. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a real-world application in astrophysics for predicting binary asteroid orbits.

The current methods for COVID-19 detection rely heavily on host macrophages, which often appear without distinct features of Inflammation or Fibrosis tissue, causing a significant imbalance between the number of true positives and false positives in detection results. To address this issue, this research proposes a new framework that incorporates a neutral tissue prior to improve the learning process for COVID-19 detection. The framework consists of two parts: the first converts ambiguous image boundaries into precise lesion areas and the second refines the detection process using a combination of a neutral prior and a previously defined Inflammation/ Fibrosis prior. The performance of the proposed framework was tested using the public EMICD dataset and this method achieved an AUC of 92.11 for virus detection, which is 1.44% higher than the baseline AUC, with an average PSNR increase of 12.15 dB in segmentation precision, demonstrating its superiority over the baseline results.

Accurately identifying vertebrae in spinal CT images is crucial for treating and diagnosing conditions, although it's hindered by clear radiological image views due to the 3D nature of the spine. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a sophisticated method that corrects image distortions and amplifies the spine area for easier detection. By initially rectifying the image to minimize distortion and cut off areas not containing the spine, we can then enhance the spine region, making vertebrae easier to distinguish. Building on this modified image, our model accurately positions and identifies vertebrae by leveraging features learned from enhanced spine regions. Through thorough testing on standard datasets, we found our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in identifying vertebrae, achieving up to 2% better results.

The novel regime of light-matter interaction has sparked considerable interest, characterized by ultrastrong, weak, or intermediate coupling. This new perspective emerges from minimizing a fundamental parameter: the electron-photon mass ratio. This can be achieved by surrounding electrons with other particles that have a negligible photon-electron interaction. This work theoretically explores a scenario where electrons are surrounded by a cavity containing bosons with a negligible photon-electron interaction. When the cavity bosons oscillate, they induce a stabilization mechanism for the electron's excited states through a resonance phenomenon. These results can also be applied to other systems, such as atom-ion plasmon scattering, providing a new pathway for ion storage research.

In recent years, quadruped robots equipped with flexible actuators are gaining popularity, thanks to their advantages in size, weight, and cost. However, the flexibility of these actuators can also cause issues, particularly during mobility tasks. To address this challenge, this research focuses on finding the most effective way to control the flexible actuators in quadruped robots, specifically when navigating flat surfaces. We developed an innovative method that enables accurate modeling of flexible actuators based on data, which when combined with existing quadruped control techniques, enables stable and efficient movement. We tested our approach on an actual robot called Mr.Cubot, and compared its performance with other existing approaches, leading to notable improvements in mobility.

A fundamental concept in quantum dynamics is the divisibility principle, which essentially asks whether a quantum state can be broken down into multiple smaller states without any residual influence remaining. While exact proof is lacking in most scenarios, a recent approach provides insight into the extent of state divisibility using a specific target goal in mind. Specifically, it involves determining whether a quantum state can be split into multiple smaller states without any residual influence. A new variational method has been developed to tackle this problem, and in practical terms, it translates to finding the tightest bounds possible for specific quantum norms. Initially, the approach is demonstrated using simple quantum systems but shows remarkable precision when applied to more complex Bell-diagonal states, some of which have previously been shown not to be fully divisible, while others have remained unclear in this regard.

A well-documented phenomenon in solar and stellar atmospheric science is the miniflare phenomenon, characterized by localized magnetic eruptions, small-scale spitting of threads, and subsequent interaction with global magnetic fields, though the exact cause behind these magnetic eruptions remains unknown. Researchers have investigated this phenomenon by creating small-scale, three-dimensional plasma simulations in a lab setting, using electrons and ions in a grid to study their behavior. They discovered that in the absence of collisions, electron temperature rises uniformly within the simulation area, but at a varying rate, with hotter regions experiencing a faster rate of temperature increase. This temperature increase leads to the growth of Kelvin-Helmholtz-like surface instabilities, causing fluctuations in the plasma surface and ultimately resulting in complete magnetic disruption. This phenomenon offers a potential explanation for the observed miniflare geometry and is an area where laboratory-scale experiments may provide valuable insights, given that real-world plasma instabilities drive the observed magnetic disruption.

The primary goal of fashion image retrieval is to enable users to locate fashion images based on specified attributes, such as garments, accessories, or styles. To facilitate this process, researchers often collect and annotate a set of fashion images with predefined traits, which are used as a basis for training a model to predict unseen image traits. However, the current approaches face limitations in efficiently utilizing the readily available feature-level annotations, leading to a gap in the community for developing effective feature-level trait prediction methods. To address this issue, we present a semi-supervised framework for feature-level trait manipulation. By employing feature-level annotations as local manipulability constraints, the framework allows for modifying the pre-trained CNN features in both fashion and non-fashion datasets to achieve reliable trait-level control. Additionally, the framework supports multiple manipulation tasks, including the alignment of image styles across different domains, which is demonstrated through semi-supervised fashion image retrieval experiments on the ZALESI dataset, as well as an interesting style transfer experiment between fashion images and the entire training set of Labeled Dataset of Images on e-Bay (LIIE) with only 250 annotations.

The Swerling model, a mathematical representation in a Hilbert space, has been used to approximate radiation patterns of aircraft under linear constraints. However, when this model becomes ill-posed, small changes in the data lead to excessively large variations in the solution, making the problem mathematically intractable. To mitigate this, a dual gradient ascent method is employed in a Banach space framework to smooth the cost function, thereby ensuring the existence of a gradient. Our approach uses a smooth penalty function with an adjoint operator and demonstrates penalty parameter independence. Furthermore, we provide convergence rates for the gradient method under a Lipschitz condition.

Determining the depth of a four-dimensional light field image, also known as light field depth, is crucial for generating depth information and enhancing the visual effects of images with four dimensions. Researchers have proposed various methods for estimating the depth of light field images, but these techniques typically perform well on standard datasets and poorly on datasets with occlusions. In response to this challenge, we introduce the Occlusion-Responsive Cross-Diversity loss (OCR loss) to enhance the diversity of images and facilitate learning in regions affected by occlusions. The OCR loss is designed to work with other existing light field depth estimation losses and can be used with different variants. Experiments using different variants of the OCR loss were conducted and compared with state-of-the-art approaches for estimating the depth of light field images. Notably, our approach outperforms existing methods, and we publicly share our code and dataset to facilitate learning for images with occlusions.

This study applies the bilinear method to derive a novel set of hidden identity-type equations for the Fokas-Lenells equations, thereby confirming a recently proposed conjecture relating these equations to the Fokas-Lenells system through a reduced system approach.

A novel approach to gauge theories of gravity that generalizes the standard Riemannian action is proposed, inspired by novel phase transitions. The approach is illustrated by applying it to specific cosmological models, including a model similar to the Lambert cube, for which mathematical formulas to derive related field theories are provided.

To meet growing data demands and improve network performance, service providers are incorporating more advanced WiFi management tools. However, these resources are underutilized in home networks due to a lack of awareness among users. We suggest using IEEE 802.11k/v standards to gather real-time data and make informed decisions about AP and extender configuration. A load measurement mechanism is proposed that can be shared across devices, allowing a centralized service to optimize home networks by deploying the IEEE 802.11k/v standards' features. A, Load estimation mechanism 'B' is proposed. By leveraging these tools, a service provider can offer users control and visibility over their networks, leading to improved network efficiency and reduced costs. We tested our service model and found it to be more effective than current methods at regulating WiFi networks.
